evidence_set: Table 3 is presented as published clinical cases involving hyponatraemia after phenethylamines. The independent reader's count of the printed table is 52 rows from 1991-2018, 46 female and 6 male, ages 13-49 with one age unknown; 50 rows are labelled MDMA (including Molly described as pure MDMA), one methamphetamine and one ethcathinone with methylone. Outcomes are labelled Death in 21 rows, Recovery in 27, Unknown in 3, and are blank in 1. Numeric sodium appears in 36 rows and is absent in 16; the lowest reported value within each of the 36 rows ranges from 101 to 130 mmol/L. One of these rows reports 137 on day one and 129 on day three, so the range of all printed sodium values is 101-137 mmol/L, without adding a case. Ten Death-labelled rows report sodium, 109-126 mmol/L, within the 101-130 mmol/L range of the lowest per-row values in the 24 Recovery-labelled rows with sodium. Amount is Unknown or blank in 30 rows, including 14 of the 21 Death-labelled rows, and numeric drug concentrations appear in 4 rows. Nine MDMA-labelled rows list at least one additional substance; six of these list an additional substance other than MDA, while the remaining three list MDA alone in addition to MDMA. Ten Death-labelled rows, nine female and one male, cite Rosenson 2007, whose bibliography entry identifies the California series: these are citation overlap with that series, not deaths independently ascertained by this review. These are table counts, not verified unique patients or population rates.
Table 3, all 52 printed rows on PDF/printed pp. 5-6; Section 5 continuation on p. 7; reader414 manual transcription and recomputation (table3_reader414.json; arithmetic_reader414.json).

Table 3 contains two pairs of female rows attributed to Matthai 1996 and Wilkins 1996 with matching ages 15/16, sodium 119/112 mmol/L and Recovery outcomes; one Matthai row additionally lists MDA. They appear to be repeated case entries, but the primary reports were not read and patient identity is unverified. The Wilkins bibliography entry on p. 14 has the same cerebral-oedema/unrestricted-water topic and includes an author reply; this suggests correspondence on the report, but the entry does not expressly label it a letter. Conditionally omitting the two Wilkins rows leaves 50 rows and 44 female rows, not a verified distinct-patient sample. The female age-23, sodium-123 mmol/L Recovery row cites Chen and Viola 1991, whose bibliography title instead concerns a laboratory method for detecting ras point mutations. The fatal row cited only as 2001 resolves within the review to its first bibliography entry, A fatal case of Ecstasy poisoning, Paediatr Child Health 6(7), 491, DOI 10.1093/pch/6.7.491, PMCID PMC2807764. Three Death-labelled rows (Karlovsek 2005 twice; Libiseller 2005) provide neither numeric sodium nor a hyponatraemia effect label. The O'Connor 1999 row has a blank outcome even though its bibliography title reports a death; the table count remains 21 Death labels and one blank, rather than 22 primary-source-confirmed deaths. The Salathe 2018 row is labelled methamphetamine although its bibliography title names ecstasy. These are internal discrepancies or probable duplicate entries, not corrections verified from the unseen primary reports. The four rows reporting numeric drug concentrations do not establish that every other case lacked toxicological testing.

Table 3 on pp. 5-6 (reader414 rows 1, 22-24, 33, 36, 44-47, 52); Section 5 continuation on p. 7; anonymous 2001 entry on p. 12; Chen/Viola, Karlovsek and Libiseller entries on p. 13; Matthai, O'Connor, Salathe and Wilkins entries on p. 14.
